title: The Law of Demeter: Stop Chaining Methods
partialText:
Every dot in a method chain is a dependency you didn’t intend to write.

The mock that ate your morning

You are writing a test for a function that generates a shipping label. The function needs the city. It gets it like this:

def generate_label(order) -> str:
    return f"Ship to: {order.customer.address.city}"

You write the test:

from unittest.mock import MagicMock

order = MagicMock()
order.customer.address.city = "London"

label = generate_label(order)
print(label)
Ship to: London

Three weeks later, the Customer class gets refactored. Shipping and billing addresses are now separate objects. customer.address becomes customer.shipping_address. You update Customer. You update generate_label. Then you search the codebase for customer.address and find six more test files with mock setups that chain through it. You update all six. One of them had a typo in the mock path and was never actually asserting what you thought…you only discover this after production ships wrong postcodes for two days.

The chain was readable. It was also a dependency on the internal structure of three objects you did not own, distributed invisibly across six test files.

By the end of this article, you will be able to identify Law of Demeter violations in your own code, understand the coupling they create, and apply the Tell, Don’t Ask refactoring to eliminate them without rewriting large parts of your codebase.

What the Law of Demeter actually says

The Law of Demeter was formulated at Northeastern University in 1987. The formal rule: a method M on object O should only call methods on:

  1. O itself
  2. Objects passed as parameters to M
  3. Objects M creates or instantiates
  4. O’s direct component objects (its attributes)

Everything else, objects you reach through calling a method on one of the above, is off limits.

The common shorthand is “use only one dot.” That shorthand is wrong, and it causes people to dismiss the principle as a style rule.

"hello world".strip().lower().split() uses three dots. It does not violate the Law of Demeter. All three method calls are on the same str object, or on the return value of the previous call on that same object. You are not navigating through a foreign object’s internals.

The correct test: are you reaching into an object you were given in order to extract an internal object, and then acting on that internal object?

order.customer.address.city fails this test. You asked order for its customer, then asked customer for its address, then asked address for its city. Each step reaches through a layer of encapsulation you do not own.

The cost: coupling and its consequences

When you chain through three objects, you encode three structural assumptions in every caller:

  • Order has a customer attribute
  • customer has an address attribute
  • address has a city attribute

When Customer is refactored, every caller that chains through it breaks:

# Before refactoring
city = order.customer.address.city

# After: Customer now has shipping_address and billing_address
city = order.customer.shipping_address.city  # every caller to update

With Tell, Don’t Ask (covered in the next section), the chain collapses to a single method on Order. When Customer is refactored, you update Order.shipping_city in one place. Every caller: zero changes.

The second cost is test complexity. Deep chains require deep mock setups:

from unittest.mock import MagicMock

# Six lines of setup for three lines of logic
order = MagicMock()
order.customer = MagicMock()
order.customer.address = MagicMock()
order.customer.address.city = "London"
order.customer.address.postcode = "EC1A 1BB"

Each line is another place that breaks either silently or noisily when the chain changes. With Tell, Don’t Ask, the mock collapses to two lines:

order = MagicMock()
order.shipping_city.return_value = "London"
order.shipping_postcode.return_value = "EC1A 1BB"

Tell, Don’t Ask

The refactoring pattern that fixes Law of Demeter violations is called Tell, Don’t Ask.

Asking means reaching into an object to extract a value and then acting on it yourself:

# Asking — you pull the value out and act on it
city = order.customer.address.city
label = f"Ship to: {city}"

Telling means giving the responsibility to the object that owns the data:

from __future__ import annotations

class Order:
    def __init__(self, customer: Customer) -> None:
        self.customer = customer

    def shipping_city(self) -> str:
        return self.customer.address.city  # violation is now inside Order, not spread across callers

class Customer:
    def __init__(self, address: Address) -> None:
        self.address = address

class Address:
    def __init__(self, city: str, postcode: str) -> None:
        self.city = city
        self.postcode = postcode

address = Address(city="London", postcode="EC1A 1BB")
customer = Customer(address=address)
order = Order(customer=customer)

def generate_label(order: Order) -> str:
    return f"Ship to: {order.shipping_city()}"  # one hop, no foreign internals

print(generate_label(order))

The violation still exists inside Order.shipping_city — self.customer.address.city is a two-dot chain. But it is now contained. There is one place in the codebase that knows the Customer → Address → city path. All callers see only order.shipping_city().

When Customer is refactored to shipping_address, you update Order.shipping_city. One change. Twelve callers: zero changes.

A second example: configuration chains

Configuration objects are one of the most common sources of Law of Demeter violations in Python:

class Pipeline:
    def __init__(self, config: "Config") -> None:
        self.config = config

    def connect(self) -> None:
        conn_str = self.config.db.connection_string  # violation
        self._db = Database(conn_str)

Pipeline depends on Config’s internal structure: that it has a db attribute, and that db has a connection_string. Two fixes:

Option 1: Delegate to Config — use this when Pipeline genuinely uses Config for multiple settings and keeping the relationship makes sense.

class DBConfig:
    def __init__(self, connection_string: str) -> None:
        self.connection_string = connection_string

class Config:
    def __init__(self, db: DBConfig) -> None:
        self.db = db

    def db_connection_string(self) -> str:
        return self.db.connection_string  # chain contained here

class Pipeline:
    def __init__(self, config: Config) -> None:
        self.config = config

    def connect(self) -> None:
        conn_str = self.config.db_connection_string()  # one hop
        print(f"Connecting with: {conn_str}")

config = Config(db=DBConfig("postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb"))
Pipeline(config=config).connect()
Connecting with: postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb

Option 2: Inject the dependency directly — use this when Pipeline only ever needs one value from Config. This breaks the dependency on Config entirely.

class DBConfig:
    def __init__(self, connection_string: str) -> None:
        self.connection_string = connection_string

class Config:
    def __init__(self, db: DBConfig) -> None:
        self.db = db

class Pipeline:
    def __init__(self, connection_string: str) -> None:
        self._connection_string = connection_string

    def connect(self) -> None:
        print(f"Connecting with: {self._connection_string}")

# Chain appears once, at the composition root
config = Config(db=DBConfig("postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb"))
Pipeline(connection_string=config.db.connection_string).connect()
Connecting with: postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb

Option 2 is often the cleaner design: Pipeline no longer needs to know Config exists. But Option 1 is the right choice when Pipeline is legitimately Config-aware and receives multiple values from it — injecting every individual value would produce a constructor with ten parameters.

What is not a violation

Not every multi-dot expression violates the Law of Demeter.

Chaining on the same object is fine:

# All on the same str — no foreign objects traversed
result = "  Hello World  ".strip().lower().replace(" ", "_")
print(result)
hello_world

The test: are you navigating through an object to reach its internals, or are you calling methods on an object that is directly in scope? str.strip() returns a new str. str.lower() is called on that str. You never reach into a foreign object’s internals.

Gotchas

Properties can hide violations — and that is sometimes fine. A common first step is wrapping the chain in a property:

class Order:
    @property
    def customer_city(self) -> str:
        return self.customer.address.city  # violation moved, not removed

This improves all callers (order.customer_city instead of order.customer.address.city) and localises the coupling to one place. That is a real improvement, and it is a legitimate intermediate step — especially when you have many callers to update. Know that you have not eliminated the coupling, only consolidated it. If Customer’s internals change, Order.customer_city still breaks. The property is not the final answer; it is the right stopping point when full Tell, Don’t Ask would require more structural change than the problem warrants right now.

Don’t build a facade for everything. Adding order.customer_first_name(), order.customer_email(), order.customer_address_line_1() … for every conceivable access pattern is worse than the original chain. Apply LoD where change is likely where one side of the chain may evolve independently of the other. Don’t apply it mechanically to every dot in the codebase.

ORMs are a structural exception. order.customer.address.city in Django or SQLAlchemy is a deliberate design choice, the chain is lazy-loaded and the ORM provides the migration tooling. You are making a coupling trade-off, and the ORM team owns the consequences. Know that you are making the trade.

Takeaways

  • The Law of Demeter says: only call methods on objects you directly know — not on objects you reach through calling a method on something else.
  • Every dot that crosses an object boundary is a structural dependency — a place that breaks when any object in the chain changes.
  • Deep chains also produce deep mocks: verbose setup that breaks silently or noisily in multiple places when the chain changes.
  • The fix is Tell, Don’t Ask: move the traversal inside the object that owns the data, expose a method that returns what callers need.
  • A property wrapper is a useful intermediate step — it consolidates coupling in one place without eliminating it.
  • Apply LoD at stability boundaries. Don’t add facade methods for every access path.

Where to go next

Most Law of Demeter violations arise because no single object owns the concept the caller needs. When you find yourself traversing order.customer.address.city, it is often because Order hasn’t been given responsibility for shipping. That is an SRP boundary waiting to be drawn: Single Responsibility Principle in Python.

For the configuration chain specifically, where injection is cleaner than delegation, the Dependency Inversion Principle article covers why injecting at the composition root produces more testable and stable code: Dependency Inversion Principle in Python.

If you found this post helpful, don’t forget to 👏 clap to show your support!

I’d also love to hear your thoughts and insights on the techniques covered in this article. 💡 Feel free to share your experiences in the comments 💬.

Connect with Me on LinkedIn!

You can also connect with me on LinkedIn for updates on my latest posts and projects. 🌐 Let’s keep the conversation going!

title: FAANG : Delete 1 Million Rows. The Real Problem Wasn’t Deleting Them.
partialText:
Most engineers focus on the DELETE statement. Production systems care about everything that happens after it.

The requirement looked simple.

Delete 1 million rows from a production orders table — older records, no longer needed, taking up storage.

The first instinct was immediate:

DELETE FROM orders
WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01';

Done. Clean. Obvious.

In a development environment, it works perfectly. Runs in seconds on a small dataset, rows disappear, life goes on.

Production environments are not development environments. That’s the lesson this problem teaches, and it teaches it expensively.

What That Statement Actually Does In Production

The issue isn’t the SQL syntax. The issue is what a database has to do to execute it.

A DELETE on a large table isn’t just removing rows. It acquires locks — row locks, index locks, potentially page locks depending on the database. It writes to the transaction log, because every deleted row needs to be recoverable until the transaction commits. It updates every secondary index that references the deleted rows. And it holds all of that open for the entire duration of the operation.

One million rows with a reasonable secondary index structure might take twenty minutes. Forty minutes. Longer, depending on I/O throughput and what else is running concurrently.

During those forty minutes, other transactions that need to touch the same rows wait. Writes queue up. Reads that hit locked rows either wait or return errors. The application doesn’t go down — but it starts feeling like it did. Response times climb. Timeouts appear. The database is technically available; the application effectively isn’t.

Availability isn’t binary. That’s the first thing this problem reveals.

“Just Run It At Midnight”

The natural instinct is to schedule the operation during off-peak hours.

This works for a lot of systems. If traffic genuinely drops at 2 AM in a single timezone, a maintenance window is reasonable.

The problem is that most systems at any meaningful scale aren’t single-timezone. A global application doesn’t have a midnight — there’s always a region in the middle of business hours. And even for systems with genuine quiet periods, a delete job that was supposed to take thirty minutes and actually takes three hours doesn’t respect the schedule you planned around.

Maintenance windows don’t scale. Leaning on them as a primary strategy means you’re one unexpectedly slow operation away from a production incident.

Indexes Solve Half The Problem

When a bulk delete is slow, the first instinct is to check whether created_at is indexed. Often it isn't. Without an index, the database scans the entire table to find matching rows — painful on a large table, and adding the index makes the deletion faster.

It isn’t fully solved. An index reduces search cost. It doesn’t meaningfully reduce the cost of deletion itself.

Every deleted row still has to be removed from every secondary index that references it. Transaction logs still grow with each delete. The replication stream still has to carry every row removal downstream. The lock duration improves because the database finds rows faster, but the fundamental work — updating all data structures for one million removals — is still happening.

Indexes are necessary. They’re just not sufficient.

Batching: The Standard Answer — And The Thing Engineers Miss Right After It

The standard production approach is batching: instead of deleting one million rows in a single transaction, delete a thousand at a time in a loop.

DELETE FROM orders
WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 1000;

Add a small sleep between iterations — even 100ms — and the behavior changes dramatically. Each transaction is small. Locks are held briefly and released. The transaction log has time to flush. Other operations get interleaved between batches. Recovery, if something goes wrong, means restarting from the last completed batch rather than rolling back an hour of work.

At this point, most engineers feel they’ve solved the problem. In many companies, they probably have.

But production systems have a habit of exposing the thing you forgot to measure.

Part of a series on system design, production engineering, and the interview questions that reveal how engineers actually think under pressure. And if you’re preparing for practical engineering interviews or trying to improve production-level thinking beyond just solving DSA problems, I’ve also been exploring platforms like PracHub.

The Problem That Lives On The Replica

The primary database handles batch deletes well. Each batch is small, locks release quickly, traffic continues with minimal disruption.

Meanwhile, every one of those deletes — all one million, across all batches — gets written to the binary log and shipped to every read replica. The replicas have to replay each delete. They’re doing the same work, just later, while simultaneously serving live read traffic.

If the primary is running through batches quickly and replicas are already under load, they fall behind. Replication lag climbs. Reads on replicas start returning data that’s minutes old.

Here’s what that looks like from a user’s perspective: a customer deletes an order and immediately refreshes the page. Their request hits a replica that’s five minutes behind. The order reappears. They try to delete it again. The primary is completely healthy. The replica is just behind. From the outside, it’s indistinguishable from a bug.

This is often more disruptive in practice than lock contention on the primary, because it’s harder to diagnose. Primary metrics look fine. It takes checking replication lag explicitly to see what’s happening.

What makes it easy to miss is that most monitoring setups track the primary by default. Replica lag is usually a separate metric you have to go looking for.

A production-grade bulk delete needs replication lag as a first-class concern — throttle or pause the job if lag climbs past a threshold, resume when replicas catch up. That’s not an edge case concern. For any system with read replicas and any meaningful delete volume, it’s the main concern.

One More Surprise For PostgreSQL Users

PostgreSQL engineers sometimes encounter an unexpected result after a large batch delete: the table is still roughly the same size on disk.

When PostgreSQL deletes rows, it marks them as dead tuples rather than immediately reclaiming the space. The rows are invisible to new queries, but the space they occupied stays within the table’s data files. It becomes reusable for future inserts — but it isn’t returned to the operating system until VACUUM processes the table.

For a one-million-row delete, the expected storage recovery might not appear for hours, or until a VACUUM FULL runs — which has its own locking implications. Engineers who delete a large table expecting immediate disk relief sometimes find themselves investigating a "storage problem" that isn't one.

The Question That Changes Everything

Here’s a question worth asking before any of the above: why is this data being deleted?

This sounds like process overhead. In practice, it occasionally changes the solution entirely.

If old data is removed on a regular schedule — every month, every quarter, every year — this isn’t really a deletion problem. It’s a data lifecycle problem. Framed that way, the natural solution isn’t a delete job that runs periodically and fights with production traffic. It’s a table designed for deletion from the start.

Partitioning by date — a separate physical partition for each month or year — turns deletion into a single metadata operation:

ALTER TABLE orders DROP PARTITION p_2023;

That takes seconds. It doesn’t touch indexes. It doesn’t write to the transaction log. It doesn’t generate replication events proportional to row count. The database removes the partition definition and reclaims the storage. One line, essentially instant, regardless of how many rows were in that partition.

The catch is that partitioning has to be designed in from the beginning, or retrofitted with significant effort on a live table. The lesson experienced engineers carry from this: if data will need periodic deletion, design for it when the table is created. The best delete strategy is sometimes a decision made years before the delete ever runs.

If the reason for deletion is compliance — data must not exist past a certain date — archival tables are worth considering before going straight to DELETE. Move rows to orders_archive, then delete from the archive at a controlled pace. The original records are preserved until the archive is cleared, which gives a recovery window if the requirement turns out to be more nuanced than the ticket described.

If the reason is query performance rather than storage, deletion might not be the answer at all. Archiving rarely-accessed rows or adjusting query patterns might solve the performance issue without the operational overhead of a large delete.

What Happens When The Job Fails At Row 800,000?

A batch delete job runs for several hours, makes it through 800,000 rows, and then fails — deployment restart, database timeout, anything. Now what?

If the job isn’t designed for resumability, the options are restart from the beginning or figure out manually where it left off. If no progress is tracked anywhere, “figure out manually” is harder than it sounds.

A production-grade delete job tracks which ID range or batch it last completed. It’s idempotent — running a batch twice doesn’t cause problems. It emits metrics: rows deleted, current deletion rate, replication lag on each iteration. It can be paused and resumed deliberately, not just on failure.

This is the shift that separates a one-time SQL command from a production operational workflow. Bulk data changes at this scale are long-running processes. They need to be treated like one.

What This Problem Is Really About

Some engineers often focus on whether an operation works.

Good engineers spend more time thinking about what happens while it’s working.

The DELETE statement takes one line. Keeping the business running while it executes — managing locks, monitoring replicas, handling storage reclamation, building a resumable job, understanding why the data is being removed in the first place — that’s the real design challenge.

The SQL is the easy part.

Everything around it is where the engineering actually lives.

Encountered something like this in production? I’d enjoy hearing what you ran into in the comments.

Part of a series on system design, production engineering, and the interview questions that reveal how engineers actually think under pressure. And if you’re preparing for practical engineering interviews or trying to improve production-level thinking beyond just solving DSA problems, I’ve also been exploring platforms like PracHub.

title: PICO-8: The Fantasy Console for People Who Actually Want to Finish a Game
partialText:
A developer’s logbook on the tiny tool that brings game dev back to its essence.

This article was originaly published in French on my website: NX Academy. Since I wrote only in French on NX, I decided to publish an English version here on Medium.

A few weeks ago, I took part in my very first game jam on itch.io. I won’t dwell on it here: I’ll come back to it in another article. But in short: I loved it, and I learned a huge amount in very little time.

I built my game with MonoGame. It’s a pretty cool C# framework. It lets you do a lot, but it’s a big tool. To ship the game, I quickly found myself juggling several other programs on the side: Aseprite for the sprites and spritesheets, and Sonic Pi for the music. It wasn’t insurmountable but, honestly, that was a lot of pieces to assemble before even writing the first line of gameplay.

It was while trying to lighten all of that, after the jam, that I stumbled onto PICO-8. And there, it just clicked. Within minutes, I understood the tool’s potential: everything is in one place. You code, you draw, you compose, you play. All without leaving the program.

A heads-up: this article isn’t a tutorial or a technical reference. For now, it’s more of a “logbook”, or, in other words, the field notes of a developer discovering PICO-8 and wanting to share why he finds the tool so clever. If you’re curious about game dev, a beginner, or simply someone who’d love to finally finish a game, you should find something for you here.

What is PICO-8?

PICO-8 is what’s called a fantasy console. Basically, it’s a game console that never existed. Nobody ever manufactured the machine. Its creator simply invented its specs, like a tiny screen, a handful of colors, a minuscule amount of memory, with the idea of recreating the spirit of old consoles. The “retro” feel of the console isn’t an accident tied to age. It’s a genuine design choice, embraced from start to finish.

When you launch PICO-8, you land in a small environment where everything is gathered together. You can run games, code your own, draw your sprites, build your maps and compose your music. You can do all of that in one place, without installing a single extra tool. PICO-8 bakes the code, music, sound, sprite and map editors directly into the console. It’s a bit like an IDE for video games: a single environment that centralizes everything.

To use it, I bought the paid version from the official site. It’s software that runs on your computer (Windows, Mac or Linux) for around $15. If you just want to try the tool before pulling out your credit card, know that there’s also a free education edition: a stripped-down version of PICO-8 officially made by Lexaloffle, playable straight in the browser. For my part, I didn’t test it; I went all in right away.

On the code side, you program your games in Lua. I find this language very readable. To give you a reference point, in spirit it reminded me a little of Ruby. Nothing intimidating: it’s a lightweight language you pick up fast.

What kinds of games can you make?

Quite a lot, actually, as long as you stick to small formats. You can make platformers, puzzlers, shoot’em ups, small roguelikes or mini-RPGs. Here, the common denominator isn’t the genre, it’s the scale. PICO-8 is built for short, complete games: the kind of game you finish in one session and, above all, that you finish at all. Because the code size is deliberately limited, games stay compact: you can play them and beat them in one sitting.

This whole little world lives in an already well-stocked ecosystem. PICO-8 ships with a built-in cartridge browser to explore what others have created. On top of that, most of these games play directly in the browser. It’s hard to make sharing or discovering a game any simpler.

Personally, I mostly see PICO-8 as a fantastic prototyping tool. The idea: quickly put together a playable prototype, share it, gather feedback, and start building a community around your concept. If the potential is there, nothing stops you from later moving to a beefier toolchain (MonoGame, Aseprite and friends) to turn it into a more ambitious “commercial” version.

The perfect example here is Celeste. The original game (now called Celeste Classic) was developed in PICO-8 by Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry in just four days, as part of a game jam, back in 2016. That little prototype went on to become one of the most acclaimed indie platformers of its time: the full game shipped in January 2018, this time rebuilt in C#. One and the same idea, then — one that stands perfectly well on its own as a PICO-8 game, and that served as a springboard to a far more ambitious one. Both at once.

Why I find it interesting

PICO-8 lets me focus on the very essence of video games: game design (I’ve been reading a lot about it lately, and I’ll come back to it soon). It’s entirely possible to make a cute little game and polish your pixels. But above all, the tool pushes you to work on game feel. For example, the way a jump responds or the way movement feels crunchy and satisfying. Everything else matters less. All that’s left is the one question that really counts: is it good to play?

Being able to focus on game design is, in large part, down to the fact that everything is centralized. There’s no toolchain to set up, no back-and-forth between five programs. With PICO-8, I code, I draw, I compose, all in one place. The upshot is that I move much faster and tie myself in far fewer knots. What’s more, since you go back to the fundamentals — the game loop, sprites, collisions — without a heavy framework to tame, the feedback loop is almost instant! I tweak a line, I rerun, and I see the result within a second.

There’s also a point I find far from negligible: distribution. PICO-8 lets you export your game to HTML/JavaScript, making it playable in a browser in one click. Concretely, that means you can spread your game and get it known very quickly, without asking anyone to install anything. For a creator looking for feedback as well as a community, that’s precious.

Finally, something I care about. You can absolutely lean on AI for the code. But for the music and the sprites, you’re still largely left to get your hands dirty and make them yourself. And honestly? I think that’s great. That manual work is precisely what gives a game its personality and its character.

Constraints (and why they’re a strength)

For me, it’s constraints that give rise to the best games. That’s part of why I got into game jams. I like creating under constraint, a bit like in cooking, when you have to make do with what’s on hand rather than an infinite pantry. Having a frame is what unlocks my creativity.

And constraints are something PICO-8 has no shortage of. The screen is a small 128×128 pixel grid, the palette is fixed at 16 colors, and the code itself is limited: a cartridge (a game file) can’t exceed 8192 tokens. Basically, every word, number, parenthesis or punctuation mark counts. So you simply don’t have the room to spread yourself thin.

That’s exactly where the constraint becomes a strength. When space is tight, you stop dithering over a thousand options and you get to the essentials. It forces you back to the heart of video games, to focus on game design without letting your mind get cluttered by everything that’s superfluous. Better still: having to fit your ideas into so little space teaches you to write more efficient code and to approach every problem with creativity. The limit doesn’t curb inventiveness — it fuels it.

Let’s be honest for a second: this frame has its flip side too. PICO-8 isn’t made for sprawling games. On an ambitious project, you’ll eventually hit the token ceiling — and then you have to either optimize what’s already there or port the game to a larger platform (back to the path mentioned above). But for what PICO-8 is going for — small games with character — these limits aren’t an obstacle. They’re the playground.

A quick look at the code

Don’t panic, we’re not going to dive into a full tutorial here. I just want to show you what the skeleton of a PICO-8 game looks like, to demystify the whole thing.

It all revolves around three functions that you define, and that PICO-8 calls for you:

function _init()
  x = 0
end

function _update()
  x = x + 1
end

function _draw()
  cls()
  print("hello pico-8!", x, 60)
end

This tiny program displays the text “hello pico-8!” drifting gently to the right. And it illustrates the whole mental model:

  • _init() is called once, at startup. This is where you set up the initial state. In our case, we set the variable x to 0.
  • _update() is called on every frame, 30 times a second. It's the game's logical core: this is where you evolve the state. Here, we increment x, so the position advances frame after frame.
  • _draw() is also called on every frame, to draw. cls() clears the screen (otherwise the text would leave a trail behind it), and print() displays our message at position x on the horizontal axis, 60 pixels from the top.

The thing to remember here is this separation: on one side what changes (_update), on the other what gets shown (_draw). You never write the game loop yourself. You fill in these three slots and the engine takes care of the timing. Once you've got that, you've got the thread of almost every PICO-8 game.

What’s next?

I’m only just getting started with PICO-8, but I already know I’ll be sticking with it for a while. The tool has something addictive about it: that feeling of being able to go from idea to playable prototype in a single evening, friction-free.

I’m about to take part in a new game jam: the Retro Recreation Jam, which kicks off in a few days. The premise: take a game from before the NES era and reimagine it your own way. I already have my idea in mind, but I’ll tell you more about it very soon.

In the meantime, if this article has made you want to try PICO-8, don’t overthink it: fire up the free version in your browser, type a couple of lines, and see where it takes you. That’s often how the best stories begin.

Resources

  • The official PICO-8 site, to buy the tool and explore the console: lexaloffle.com/pico-8.
  • The official manual, which covers the whole API as well as the built-in editors’ functions: the PICO-8 manual.

title: Stop Adding Indexes to Fix Slow Queries — You’re Quietly Killing Your Writes
partialText:
Every index you add is a tax. Most teams only ever count the discount.

There’s a moment almost every backend engineer has lived through.

A query is slow. Someone opens a dashboard, sees a sequential scan, and does the obvious thing: adds an index. The query gets fast. Everyone moves on. A few weeks later, someone adds another. Then another. Indexes are cheap insurance, right? You add one whenever something feels slow, and you never really think about it again.

Then one day your write throughput falls off a cliff, your p99 on inserts doubles, and nobody can explain why. The queries are all fast. The dashboards are green. And yet the system feels like it’s wading through mud.

Here’s the part the tutorials skip: every index you add makes every write slower. Not a little slower in theory — measurably slower, on every single insert, update, and delete, forever. You’ve been counting the speedup on reads and silently ignoring the bill on writes.

This isn’t a database-specific quirk. It’s true in Postgres, it’s true in MongoDB, it’s true everywhere. So let’s talk about the tax you’re paying — and how to stop overpaying it.

The mental model: an index is a second copy you have to keep in sync

Strip away the B-tree internals and an index is just this: a second, sorted copy of part of your data, maintained separately from the table itself.

That’s why reads get faster — the database can jump straight to the rows it wants instead of scanning everything. But it’s also why writes get slower. The moment you change a row, the database doesn’t just write the row. It also has to go update every index that points at it, keeping each of those sorted copies correct.

One index? You write the row, then update one index. Fine. Ten indexes? You write the row, then update ten separate structures, each one a little bit of extra I/O. Your “simple insert” is now eleven writes wearing a trench coat.

MongoDB’s own documentation says it plainly: each index on a collection adds overhead, and for every insert or delete the database adds or removes the corresponding keys from each index. Postgres is the same — every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE has to maintain the indexes alongside the table.

So the real cost of an index isn’t the disk space (though that’s real too). It’s that you’ve signed up to do extra work on every write for the rest of that index’s life, in exchange for faster reads on one query shape.

That trade is often worth it. The problem is that nobody’s actually checking whether it is worth it — they’re just adding indexes whenever a read feels slow and never removing them.

The trap: indexes you’re paying for and not using

Here’s the most common version of the disease.

Someone adds an index to speed up a query. Later, the query changes — a new filter, a different sort, a refactor. The old index no longer matches the query, so the database stops using it. But the index is still there. It still gets updated on every single write. You’re paying full price and getting nothing back.

Multiply that across a few years and a few engineers, and you end up with tables carrying a dozen indexes where three are doing real work and the rest are pure overhead — dead weight that slows every write and helps no read.

If you take only one thing from this article, take this: an unused index is strictly worse than no index. It has all of the write cost and none of the read benefit. Finding and deleting those is usually the single highest-leverage database change you can make, and it costs you nothing but the courage to drop something.

That’s the whole idea, and if you stop reading here you’ve got the important part. But if you want to actually find these indexes, measure the real cost, and stop creating redundant ones — that’s the rest of the article.

Going deeper: how to find the indexes that are costing you

Both databases will tell you exactly which indexes are being used, if you ask.

MongoDB ships $indexStats, which gives you an access count per index:

db.orders.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }])

You get back something like:

[
  { name: "status_1",     accesses: { ops: 0,     since: "2026-01-01" } },
  { name: "createdAt_1",  accesses: { ops: 45230, since: "2026-01-01" } },
  { name: "legacyField_1", accesses: { ops: 0,    since: "2026-01-01" } }
]

Any index sitting at ops: 0 over a representative window — make sure you've covered a full business cycle, including the monthly report that runs at 2 a.m. — is a candidate for removal.

Postgres exposes the same truth through pg_stat_user_indexes:

SELECT relname AS table, indexrelname AS index, idx_scan AS scans
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
ORDER BY idx_scan ASC;

An index with idx_scan = 0 that's been accumulating stats for a while is, with rare exceptions, doing nothing but slowing your writes.

The one caveat for both: an index can have zero scans and still be load-bearing — a unique index enforcing a constraint, or one supporting a query that only runs quarterly. Don’t drop blindly. Confirm what each index is for before you remove it. But “what is this for?” with no good answer is your signal.

The write cost isn’t uniform — and that’s where it gets interesting

A naive reading of “every index slows every write” overstates things, and a sharp reviewer will call you on it. The reality is more nuanced, and the nuances are exactly where good index hygiene lives.

In Postgres, an update only touches the indexes whose columns actually changed. If you have an index on created_at and you update a row's status but never its created_at, that index doesn't need rewriting. Better still, Postgres has an optimization called a HOT update (heap-only tuple): when no indexed column changes and there's room on the same page, the update can skip index maintenance entirely. So a table can carry several indexes and still update cheaply — as long as your hot write path isn't touching the indexed columns.

This flips a common piece of advice. The question isn’t just “how many indexes do I have?” It’s “do my most frequent writes touch indexed columns?” An index on a column you rarely update is nearly free on writes. An index on a column you update on every single request is expensive on every single request.

Partial indexes push this further. In Postgres:

CREATE INDEX idx_active_orders ON orders (created_at)
WHERE status = 'active';

This index only needs maintenance for rows where status = 'active'. If 95% of your rows are archived, you've cut the write overhead of that index by roughly 95% while keeping it fast for the queries that only ever look at active orders. MongoDB has the same tool in partial and sparse indexes — it only updates them when the affected document actually qualifies for the index.

The lesson: before you delete an index to save write cost, ask whether you can make it smaller instead. A partial index often gives you the read you need at a fraction of the write tax.

The redundant index nobody notices

Here’s a free win that’s almost always hiding in a mature codebase.

Compound indexes work on prefixes. An index on {a: 1, b: 1} can serve queries that filter on a alone, because a is the leading column. Which means if you also have a separate index on just {a: 1}, that second index is redundant — the compound one already covers everything it does.

But the redundant {a: 1} index still gets fully maintained on every write. You're paying for two index updates to get the capability of one.

This happens constantly: someone adds {a: 1} early on, then later someone adds {a: 1, b: 1} for a new query, and nobody goes back to remove the now-pointless single-column index. Auditing for prefix-redundant indexes — in either database — routinely turns up indexes you can drop with zero loss of read performance and immediate gains on writes.

The same prefix logic is also why column order in a compound index matters enormously, but that’s a whole article of its own.

A practical audit you can run this week

You don’t need a project for this. You need about an hour.

  1. Pull index usage stats. $indexStats in MongoDB, pg_stat_user_indexes in Postgres. Make sure the stats window covers a representative period, not just the last hour.
  2. Flag the zero-use indexes. For each one, find the answer to “what query or constraint is this for?” No answer → strong drop candidate.
  3. Hunt for prefix redundancy. Any single-column index whose column is the leading field of an existing compound index is almost certainly droppable.
  4. Check your hot write path. Which columns get updated most often? Indexes on those are your most expensive ones — make sure each is genuinely earning its keep, and consider whether a partial index would do.
  5. Drop in staging first, measure, then production. Watch write latency and the read queries you care about. Indexes are reversible — you can always recreate one — so this is low-risk if you measure.

Do this once and most teams reclaim real write headroom they didn’t know they’d given away.

The takeaway

Indexes aren’t free, and they aren’t a default. Each one is a standing trade: faster reads on a specific query shape, paid for with slower writes on every operation that touches it, forever. That trade is frequently worth making — but only if you’re actually making it deliberately, and only as long as the read benefit still exists.

Most slow-write mysteries aren’t mysteries. They’re a pile of indexes that someone added to fix a read months ago, that no longer match any query, quietly taxing every write in the system.

Stop adding indexes reflexively. Start auditing the ones you have. The fastest write is the one that doesn’t have to update an index nobody’s reading from.

If you found this useful, the same “you’re probably doing it wrong” energy is in my piece on why storing JWTs in localStorage is a security mistake — same instinct, different layer of the stack.

https://levelup.gitconnected.com/stop-using-jwt-for-authentication-the-way-you-learned-it-e96af029f256

title: Stop Installing Every Node.js Module Up Front: A Better Architecture for On-Demand Dependencies
partialText:
How to design Node.js applications that reference optional modules, install or load them only when needed, and keep dependency governance under control.

Most Node.js applications treat dependencies as a fixed up-front cost.

If a feature might need a package, we add it to package.json, install it during setup, and load it when the application starts or when a file is imported. That works well for small projects, but it becomes painful as applications grow.

Over time, the dependency tree becomes heavier. Install times increase. Cold starts slow down. Optional features quietly become mandatory. Packages used by one rarely visited workflow are installed for every user, every environment, and every deployment.

There is a better pattern:

Application code should depend on capabilities, not packages.

Instead of importing a package directly, a feature should request a capability. The application can then decide whether that capability is already available, whether it needs to be installed, whether it is allowed, and how it should be injected.

This is the idea behind On-Demand Module Injection for Node.js.

The Problem With Standard Node.js Dependency Loading

In a standard Node.js application, we usually do something like this:

import sharp from "sharp";

That line looks innocent, but it creates a hard dependency.

The application now assumes:

  • sharp is installed
  • the correct native binaries are available
  • the module is needed in this environment
  • the feature using it is part of the current runtime path
  • every deployment should carry that dependency

For core functionality, that is fine. For optional functionality, it is often wasteful.

Examples of optional dependencies include:

  • image processing
  • PDF generation
  • Markdown rendering
  • YAML parsing
  • AI provider SDKs
  • database adapters
  • cloud storage adapters
  • payment provider integrations
  • analytics exporters

Many applications have features that only some users or environments need. Yet the default dependency model installs everything for everyone.

The Architecture: On-Demand Module Injection

The architecture is simple:

Application code
   ↓
Feature asks for a capability
   ↓
Module registry checks if a provider is available
   ↓
If installed: import it
If missing: install or download it
   ↓
Validate the module
   ↓
Inject it into the feature
   ↓
Cache it for later use

The feature does not say:

import marked from "marked";

It says:

const markdown = await modules.resolve("markdown");

That small change creates a powerful boundary.

The application is no longer tightly coupled to a package. It is coupled to a capability. The registry owns the package-level details.

Core Components

This architecture has five main parts.

1. A Module Manifest

The manifest declares which capabilities the application supports and which npm packages provide them.

{
  "modules": {
    "markdown": {
      "package": "marked",
      "version": "^12.0.0",
      "entry": "marked",
      "optional": true
    },
    "yaml": {
      "package": "yaml",
      "version": "^2.4.0",
      "entry": "yaml",
      "optional": true
    }
  }
}

This gives the application a controlled vocabulary.

Features ask for markdown or yaml. They do not decide which package to install. They do not run arbitrary imports. They do not pull package names from user input.

That matters for maintainability, and it matters even more for security.

2. A Module Registry

The registry is the central resolver.

It is responsible for:

  • reading the manifest
  • validating requested capabilities
  • checking whether a package is allowed
  • determining whether the package is installed
  • installing it when needed
  • dynamically importing it
  • caching the result

Here is a minimal reference implementation:

import fs from "node:fs/promises";
import { createRequire } from "node:module";
import { execFile } from "node:child_process";
import { promisify } from "node:util";
const execFileAsync = promisify(execFile);
const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);
export class ModuleRegistry {
  constructor({ manifestPath, allowedModules }) {
    this.manifestPath = manifestPath;
    this.allowedModules = new Set(allowedModules);
    this.cache = new Map();
  }
  async loadManifest() {
    const raw = await fs.readFile(this.manifestPath, "utf8");
    return JSON.parse(raw).modules;
  }
  async resolve(name) {
    if (this.cache.has(name)) {
      return this.cache.get(name);
    }
    const modules = await this.loadManifest();
    const config = modules[name];
    if (!config) {
      throw new Error(`Unknown module capability: ${name}`);
    }
    if (!this.allowedModules.has(config.package)) {
      throw new Error(`Package is not allowed: ${config.package}`);
    }
    await this.ensureInstalled(config.package, config.version);
    const imported = await import(config.entry);
    const moduleValue = imported.default ?? imported;
    this.cache.set(name, moduleValue);
    return moduleValue;
  }
  async ensureInstalled(packageName, version) {
    try {
      require.resolve(packageName);
      return;
    } catch {
      const spec = `${packageName}@${version}`;
      await execFileAsync("npm", ["install", spec, "--save-optional"], {
        stdio: "pipe"
      });
    }
  }
}

This is intentionally small. A production implementation should add stronger controls around installation, integrity, logging, and environment behavior.

3. An Injection Container

The registry can be exposed through a small container:

import { ModuleRegistry } from "./moduleRegistry.js";
export const modules = new ModuleRegistry({
  manifestPath: new URL("./module-manifest.json", import.meta.url),
  allowedModules: ["marked", "yaml", "pdf-lib"]
});

Feature code can now depend on the container instead of directly depending on npm packages:

import { modules } from "./container.js";
export async function renderMarkdown(input) {
  const marked = await modules.resolve("markdown");
  return marked.parse(input);
}

The feature asks for Markdown rendering. The registry decides how to satisfy that request.

4. A Lazy Installer

The installer only runs when a requested capability is missing.

For example:

npm install marked@^12.0.0 --save-optional

This can be useful in development, plugin systems, internal tools, and modular platforms where not every capability is required at startup.

However, runtime installation should be treated carefully in production. For many systems, production should use a stricter mode:

Development:
  Missing module can be installed automatically
Production:
  Missing module fails clearly, or is pulled from a controlled internal package cache

In other words, lazy loading is almost always useful. Lazy installing is environment-dependent.

5. A Security Gate

The security model is not optional.

If the application can install packages dynamically, it must never install arbitrary package names from untrusted input.

At minimum, the system should enforce:

  • declared capabilities only
  • an explicit package allowlist
  • pinned major versions
  • trusted registry configuration
  • lockfile integrity
  • audit checks in CI
  • installation logs
  • production controls
  • offline mode

The manifest is not just configuration. It is a policy boundary.

How This Fits Into package.json

For applications, optionalDependencies is a good fit:

{
  "dependencies": {
    "core-app-runtime": "^1.0.0"
  },
  "optionalDependencies": {
    "marked": "^12.0.0",
    "yaml": "^2.4.0"
  }
}

For libraries, optional peer dependencies are usually better:

{
  "peerDependencies": {
    "marked": "^12.0.0",
    "yaml": "^2.4.0"
  },
  "peerDependenciesMeta": {
    "marked": {
      "optional": true
    },
    "yaml": {
      "optional": true
    }
  }
}

The distinction matters.

Applications own their runtime. Libraries should avoid surprising the host application by installing or bundling more than necessary.

Production Structure

A production version should split responsibilities cleanly:

/core
  moduleRegistry
  manifestLoader
  installer
  integrityPolicy
  moduleCache
/features
  markdownFeature
  pdfFeature
  yamlFeature
/module-manifest.json

You can also add a small CLI:

node tools/modules.js list
node tools/modules.js install markdown
node tools/modules.js prefetch

The prefetch command is especially useful for production deployments. It allows the deployment process to install all required optional modules ahead of time while preserving the capability-based architecture at runtime.

Rollout Timeline

This can be implemented gradually.

Week 1: Prototype

Define the manifest format, build the first version of the registry, support dynamic imports, and test two optional capabilities such as Markdown and YAML.

Week 2: Feature Integration

Refactor selected features to request capabilities instead of importing packages directly. Add cache behavior and clear errors for missing, failed, or disallowed modules.

Week 3: Security and Deployment Controls

Add lockfile verification, production mode, offline mode, installation logs, and internal registry support if needed.

Week 4: Tooling and Documentation

Add CLI commands, document the manifest schema, explain how teams add optional modules, and build a small reference app.

Weeks 5–6: Hardening

Add retries, install timeouts, package integrity checks, CI policy checks, and usage telemetry.

When This Pattern Is Worth It

This architecture is useful when:

  • your application has optional features
  • install size matters
  • cold start performance matters
  • different deployments need different capabilities
  • you support plugins or extensions
  • you want stronger dependency governance
  • you need to avoid forcing every package onto every user

It may be unnecessary for small applications with a stable, minimal dependency set.

Like most architecture patterns, the value appears when the boundary solves a real problem.

Final Thought

Node.js makes it easy to install and import packages. That is one of its great strengths.

But as applications grow, direct imports can quietly turn optional capabilities into permanent obligations.

On-demand module injection gives us a cleaner model:

Feature code asks for what it needs.
The platform decides how to provide it.

That separation makes Node.js applications more modular, more adaptable, and easier to govern at scale.

The future of large Node.js systems should not be every module installed everywhere, all the time.

It should be capability-first, policy-controlled, and loaded only when needed.

title: Closing the Gap: What a Library Can’t Own
partialText:
Coordination ends at the lease store. Everything else is yours.

The fencing counter stops stale writes to the lease store. The atomic checkpoint write closes the window between progress and liveness. The handoff signal forces callers to distinguish crash recovery from intentional surrender. All three are real guarantees, and they hold.

What they don’t do is extend past the coordination layer.

That boundary is not a flaw. It is a design decision with a name. Every coordination primitive draws it somewhere — the question is whether it is drawn explicitly or discovered under load.

The fencing counter stops writes, not calls

A worker that has been superseded receives ErrFenced the next time it tries to checkpoint. It cannot corrupt the state the successor is actively building. That guarantee is real and unconditional — it rests on a single conditional write that either matches the current fencing counter or doesn't.

The guarantee does not reach external systems.

A zombie worker that woke up after its lease expired has already made its API calls, already fired its webhook, already incremented the usage counter in the billing system — before it ever tried to checkpoint. The fencing counter runs at the storage layer. It says nothing about what happened at the network layer before the stale write was rejected.

This is not a limitation of checkpointed lease handoff. It is an inherent property of any coordination primitive. A database transaction that rolls back does not undo an email that was sent inside the transaction. A Kubernetes leader election that revokes leadership does not undo the Stripe charge the previous leader placed two seconds before it was evicted. The coordination boundary is the lease store. Everything outside it is a separate problem.

The answer to that problem is not a different coordination primitive. It is making every external mutation idempotent — or using an outbox pattern to decouple the mutation from its effects entirely. Neither of those belongs in the library. Encoding them there would couple coordination semantics to application state in a way that is not generalizeable. Different callers have different external systems, different idempotency requirements, and different outbox implementations. The library draws the line at the store and stops there.

The at-least-once window is named, not closed

Between the last checkpoint write and a crash, work re-runs. Not because something went wrong with the coordination layer — the checkpoint before the crash is intact, the successor reads it, the recovery starts from exactly that point. What the successor cannot do is know whether the work that happened after the last checkpoint also had external effects that are already applied.

This is the at-least-once window. It is not a bug. It is the cost of the checkpoint granularity choice.

The window is caller-controlled. Checkpoint more frequently and the re-run window shrinks — each step is its own save boundary, and the successor re-executes one step, not ten. Checkpoint less frequently and the throughput overhead drops — fewer writes to the lease store, at the cost of more re-execution when recovery happens. The trade-off is application-specific. The library provides the mechanism. The frequency is the caller’s decision.

In the subscription cancellation example, each step writes its own checkpoint before the effect that follows it. The re-run window is one step. A system that batches ten steps before checkpointing has a larger window. Both are valid. The library does not have an opinion about which is correct — that would require knowing the cost of re-execution, the write volume, the backend capacity, and the business tolerance for duplicate effects. None of those are in scope at the coordination layer.

The checkpoint is yours — and so is the recovery logic

The library delivers two things on acquisition: []byte and a bool. The bytes are whatever the previous owner wrote as its last checkpoint. The bool says whether the previous owner released explicitly.

What those bytes mean is not the library’s concern. The library stored them. The library handed them back. The encoding, the schema, the version compatibility, the validation logic for partial state — all of that is application code. The checkpoint package provides a Codec interface and a JSON() implementation as a convenience. Using them is optional. Callers who use protobuf or a custom binary format implement Codec directly or bypass the package entirely.

The recovery logic is the same. The cleanHandoff flag says "the previous owner called Release" or "the lease expired without a release." What the caller does with that information is not the library's concern. A caller who treats both paths identically has decided that is correct for their workload. A caller who validates partial state only on crash recovery, and trusts the clean handoff checkpoint without validation, has made a different decision. Both are correct choices at the application layer. The library surfaces the distinction and stops there.

This is the same boundary the jwtauth library draws at the authentication layer. jwtauth manages the token lifecycle — issuance, rotation, revocation. It does not decide what claims belong in the token, how to validate them against business rules, or what to do when a token is presented for a resource the caller doesn't have permission to access. Those are application concerns. Encoding them in the library would make the library wrong for every caller whose rules differ from the author's assumptions.

Coordination primitives that try to own recovery logic tend to be wrong in specific ways for each caller. The library that stops at the correct boundary is useful to everyone.

Observability is what makes guarantees verifiable under load

The guarantees established in the coordination layer are claims. Under load, with real TTLs, real worker counts, and real workload characteristics, those claims need to be observable — not to verify that the library is correct, but to verify that the configuration matches the workload.

ErrFenced is the first signal. If fencing events are rare, TTLs are generous relative to work duration — workers are completing their leases before expiry in the normal case. If fencing events are frequent, TTLs are too short, or workers are too slow, or both. A system where fencing fires constantly is a system where successors are constantly re-executing work a previous owner already partially completed. That is a configuration problem, and it is invisible without the metric.

Checkpoint frequency, size, and renewal failures complete the picture. A checkpoint written once per job run has a different effect on backend throughput and recovery window size than one written per step. A renewal failure that cascades into a fencing event is a network or backend problem surfacing as a coordination event. Neither is visible without instrumentation.

The injection seam for all of this is LeaseObserver — six methods, called synchronously after each operation, carrying the token, the operation result, and in the case of OnFenced, an explicit fencing signal fired in addition to whichever of OnCheckpoint, OnRenew, or OnRelease triggered it:

type LeaseObserver interface {
    OnAcquire(ctx context.Context, e AcquireEvent)
    OnCheckpoint(ctx context.Context, e CheckpointEvent)
    OnRenew(ctx context.Context, e RenewEvent)
    OnRelease(ctx context.Context, e ReleaseEvent)
    OnReadCheckpoint(ctx context.Context, e ReadCheckpointEvent)
    OnFenced(ctx context.Context, e FencedEvent)
}

Each event struct carries the token, the operation result, and a Duration measuring the final backend call — not the wait loop for Acquire. The interface carries no opinions about exporters. A LeaseObserver that increments a Prometheus counter, one that writes structured log lines, and one that pushes to a custom metrics pipeline are all the same interface. Shipping an OpenTelemetry exporter in the library would make the library wrong for any caller using a different observability stack — and would introduce a framework dependency that contradicts the no-framework-requirements principle the library is built on. The interface is the seam. The exporter is yours.

The library extends the coordination layer with two higher-level primitives built directly on the same seam: leader, which wraps Elect for pure leader-election use cases where no checkpoint state is required, and pool, which distributes a fixed set of work IDs across competing processes with emergent rebalancing. Both inherit LeaseObserver through the Lease they receive. Getting the coordination boundary right is the easy part. Verifying that it holds under load is what the instrumentation is for.

The full examples — subscription cancellation, cluster-singleton scheduler, and partition processor — are at examples/ in the worklease repository.
